full_judgment: 9. It is now well settled that in dealing with an application for temporary injunction the foremost consideration is to determine whether the applicant has a prima facie case. But the determination of this question requires a special consideration in a suit where a judgment-debtor seeks to have a decree passed by a Court of competent jurisdiction adjudged order of the void on the ground of fraud. This is mainly for two reasons. Firstly, there being a presumption of regularity in respect of a judicial act a decree holder is presumed to have a, prima-facie title to the subject-matter of the decree and secondly, the principle of justice requires that a decree holder should not ordinarily be deprived of the fruits of the decree. A mere filing of a suit for setting-aside a decree or adjudging the same as void is no justification for an order for injunction restraining execution of a decree. Unless fraud is manifest, the Court is duty bound to examine the nature of the questions raised and their seriousness upon some materials which are indicative of the alleged fraud and considered as sufficient to rebut the presumption arising in favour of the decree holder. Of course, the Court need not enter into the merits of the case as is necessary for passing a decree after final beating. It has to tee whether a fair and arguable case exists in favour of the plaintiff or not.
